summary: Continuation of CA.3 (polynomial and matrix arithmetic) after the accepted main packet ClassicalArithmeticCompletion.json, whose CA.3 nodes it cites by id and does not repeat. It plans what that packet left open. (1) Integer-valued polynomials over Dedekind domains: the localization of Int(D) and of its characteristic ideals for Noetherian D; Newton sequences and generalized binomial bases; the Legendre exponent w_q(n); the explicit v-ordering of a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field and the resulting regular basis of Int(V); the local formula I_n(D) = ∏ 𝔪^{−w_{N(𝔪)}(n)}; factorial ideals; the ideals Π_q; the theorem that factorial ideals and the Π_q generate the same free group; the Pólya–Ostrowski criterion (Cahen–Chabert, Proposition 31); Pólya fields and the Pólya group; Ostrowski's theorem for Galois fields; the imaginary quadratic Pólya fields; and Zantema's theorem that cyclotomic fields are Pólya fields — all from public sources with proofs (Cahen–Chabert, Chabert's survey, Leriche), with the short missing proofs supplied. (2) Factor bounds for Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma: Mignotte's √m-exponent inequality (stated as quoted; Mignotte 1988 itself could not be read, a recorded gap) and the evaluation bound of their Lemma 3.4 with the corrected ‖A‖₂ ≤ H√(n+1). (3) Smith's bounded squarefree combination (Lemma 2.10) with the primitive gcd it needs, answering LogarithmicPotentialTheoryAndAlgebraicIntegers request R3. (4) Fujiwara's weighted root bound and its monic form (the accepted Bhargava–Shankar–Wang route). (5) Suppliers for the main packet's 22 review-frontier nodes: a ledger of named library declarations, and three new nodes — the Gregory–Newton expansion, a generic lower Newton polygon of a finite point family (answering ComputationalNumberTheory's CN.2 request for convex-hull, supporting-line and slope-ordering contracts), and, for CN.2's request for a finite-field kernel basis, Tau Ceti's existing computable Gauss–Jordan elimination and kernel basis (TauCeti.rowReduce, TauCeti.kernelBasis) cited, with the change-of-basis certificate and uniqueness of the reduced form and the transport of the kernel basis to a linear map in chosen bases planned on top of them.

nodes.title: Integer-valued polynomials commute with localization
nodes.statement: Let D be an integral domain with fraction field K and S ⊆ D a multiplicative set with 0 ∉ S. (i) If f ∈ K[X] satisfies f(D) ⊆ S⁻¹D, then f(S⁻¹D) ⊆ S⁻¹D; consequently S⁻¹Int(D) ⊆ Int(S⁻¹D) inside K[X]. (ii) If D is Noetherian, then S⁻¹Int(D) = Int(S⁻¹D); in particular Int(D)_𝔭 = Int(D_𝔭) for every prime 𝔭 of D. (iii) If D is Noetherian, the characteristic ideals localize: S⁻¹I_n(D) = I_n(S⁻¹D) for every n ≥ 0.
hypotheses: D an integral domain with fraction field K (Mathlib IsFractionRing D K); S a submonoid of D not containing 0, S⁻¹D the corresponding subring of K (Mathlib IsLocalization).
D Noetherian for (ii) and (iii); (i) holds for every domain. Without the Noetherian hypothesis only the inclusion S⁻¹Int(D) ⊆ Int(S⁻¹D) is asserted.
proofSteps: (i), by induction on n = deg f (Cahen–Chabert, Lemma 28): constants are clear. For a/s with a ∈ D, s ∈ S put g(X) = sⁿ f(X) − f(sX); the leading terms cancel, so deg g < n, and g(D) ⊆ S⁻¹D because sⁿ f(x) and f(sx) lie in S⁻¹D for x ∈ D. By induction g(a/s) ∈ S⁻¹D, and sⁿ f(a/s) = g(a/s) + f(a) ∈ S⁻¹D; divide by the unit sⁿ of S⁻¹D.
Inclusion: for f ∈ Int(D) and t ∈ S, f/t takes values in S⁻¹D on D, hence on S⁻¹D by (i).

(ii): let f ∈ Int(S⁻¹D). Clearing denominators, d f ∈ D[X] for some nonzero d ∈ D, so the D-submodule M of K generated by f(D) lies in d⁻¹D ≅ D. As D is Noetherian, M is generated by finitely many values f(a_1), …, f(a_r); each lies in S⁻¹D, so one t ∈ S has t f(a_j) ∈ D for all j, hence t M ⊆ D, i.e. t f ∈ Int(D) and f = (t f)/t ∈ S⁻¹Int(D).

(iii): for f ∈ Int(D) of degree n and t ∈ S, f/t ∈ Int(S⁻¹D) has degree n and leading coefficient lc(f)/t, so S⁻¹I_n(D) ⊆ I_n(S⁻¹D); conversely if g ∈ Int(S⁻¹D) has degree n, (ii) gives t ∈ S with t g ∈ Int(D) of degree n, so lc(g) ∈ t⁻¹ I_n(D).
acceptance: For D = ℤ and S = ℤ ∖ pℤ: Int(ℤ)_(p) = Int(ℤ_(p)); for example (X³ − X)/3 lies in both for p = 3, and X(X − 1)/2 lies in Int(ℤ_(3)) already because 2 is a unit there.
For D = ℤ and n = 2: I_2(ℤ_(p)) = ½ℤ_(p) is ℤ_(p) for p odd and ½ℤ_(2) for p = 2, matching I_2(ℤ) = ½ℤ localized.
The proof of (ii) uses finite generation of the module of values; it is the step where the Noetherian hypothesis enters.

nodes.title: Newton sequences and generalized binomial bases
nodes.statement: Let D be an integral domain with fraction field K and (a_n)_{n≥0} a sequence of pairwise distinct elements of D. Put f_0 = 1 and, for n ≥ 1, f_n(X) = ∏_{k<n} (X − a_k)/(a_n − a_k), the unique polynomial of degree n with f_n(a_k) = 0 for k < n and f_n(a_n) = 1. The following are equivalent: (1) every f_n lies in Int(D); (2) (f_n)_{n≥0} is a basis of the D-module Int(D) (necessarily regular: deg f_n = n); (3) for every n and every f ∈ K[X] of degree at most n, f ∈ Int(D) if and only if f(a_0), …, f(a_n) ∈ D. When they hold, (a_n) is called a Newton sequence of D, and I_n(D) = (∏_{k<n}(a_n − a_k))⁻¹ D for every n.
hypotheses: D an integral domain; the a_n pairwise distinct (so D is infinite).
proofSteps: Expansion: f_0, …, f_n is a K-basis of the polynomials of degree ≤ n (degrees 0, …, n), and every f of degree ≤ n is f = Σ_{k≤n} c_k f_k with c_k = f(a_k) − Σ_{j<k} c_j f_j(a_k): the system is triangular with unit diagonal because f_j(a_k) = 0 for k < j and f_k(a_k) = 1 (Cahen–Chabert, proof of Proposition 20).
(1) ⇒ (3): if f(a_0), …, f(a_n) ∈ D, induction on k gives c_k ∈ D because every f_j(a_k) ∈ D; so f is a D-combination of integer-valued polynomials. The converse direction of (3) is trivial.
(1) ⇒ (2): spanning is (3) applied to f ∈ Int(D); independence holds because the degrees are distinct (a nonzero combination has the degree of its top term).
(2) ⇒ (1) is trivial, and (3) ⇒ (1) because f_n takes the values 0 and 1 at a_0, …, a_n.
Characteristic ideals: (f_n) is a regular basis, so by CA.3/regular-basis-iff-characteristic-ideals-principal the leading coefficient 1/∏_{k<n}(a_n − a_k) generates I_n(D).
acceptance: D = ℤ, a_n = n: f_n is the binomial polynomial (X choose n), and the criterion is Pólya's theorem (CA.3/polya-binomial-basis) together with the test on 0, 1, …, n (CA.3/integer-valued-iff-consecutive-values); the shifted sequence a_n = a + n gives the test on any n + 1 consecutive integers.
Non-example: in D = ℤ the sequence 0, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, … is not a Newton sequence, because f_1 = X/2 is not integer-valued.
I_n(ℤ) = (1/n!)ℤ is recovered from ∏_{k<n}(n − k) = n!.

nodes.title: The Legendre exponent w_q(n)
nodes.statement: For an integer q ≥ 2 and n ∈ ℕ, w_q(n) = Σ_{k≥1} ⌊n/q^k⌋, a finite sum since its terms vanish once q^k > n. Equivalently w_q(n) = Σ_{l=1}^{n} v_q(l), where v_q(l) is the largest h with q^h | l. For a prime p, w_p(n) = v_p(n!) (Legendre's formula); for a prime power q = p^f with f ≥ 2, w_q(n) is not a p-adic valuation of n!.
hypotheses: q ≥ 2 an integer (q = 1 is excluded: the sum would diverge).
proofSteps: Define w_q(n) as the sum of n / q^k (natural-number division) over 1 ≤ k ≤ n; the terms with q^k > n vanish.
Σ_{k≥1} ⌊n/q^k⌋ counts the pairs (l, k) with 1 ≤ l ≤ n, k ≥ 1 and q^k | l, which is Σ_{l≤n} v_q(l).
Hence w_q(n + 1) − w_q(n) = v_q(n + 1), w_q(n) = 0 iff n < q, and w_q(q) = 1.
Superadditivity w_q(m) + w_q(n) ≤ w_q(m + n) termwise from ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋.
For q = p prime this is Mathlib's Legendre formula (padicValNat_factorial).
acceptance: w_q(n) = 0 for n < q.

nodes.title: The v-ordering of a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field
nodes.statement: Let V be a discrete valuation ring with normalized valuation v, maximal ideal 𝔪 = πV and finite residue field of cardinality q. Fix representatives r_0 = 0, r_1, …, r_{q−1} ∈ V of the classes of V/𝔪. For n = Σ_i n_i q^i written in base q (0 ≤ n_i < q) put a_n = Σ_i r_{n_i} π^i. Then: (a) v(a_n − a_m) = v_q(n − m) for n ≠ m; (b) for all s, h ≥ 0 the q^h consecutive terms a_s, …, a_{s+q^h−1} form a complete set of representatives of V/𝔪^h; (c) v(∏_{k<n}(a_n − a_k)) = w_q(n); (d) v(∏_{k<n}(x − a_k)) ≥ w_q(n) for every x ∈ V. In Bhargava's terms (a_n) is a v-ordering of V, and so is every shifted sequence (a_{s+n})_n.
hypotheses: V a discrete valuation ring (Mathlib IsDiscreteValuationRing) with finite residue field of cardinality q; π a uniformizer; r : Fin q → V a system of representatives of V/𝔪 with r 0 = 0.
proofSteps: (a): if n and m first differ in the base-q digit of index i, then a_n − a_m = π^i (r_{n_i} − r_{m_i}) + π^{i+1}·(element of V), and r_{n_i} − r_{m_i} is a unit, so v(a_n − a_m) = i; and i = v_q(n − m) because n ≡ m modulo q^i but not modulo q^{i+1}.
(b): among q^h consecutive indices no two are congruent modulo q^h, so by (a) no two of the a's are congruent modulo 𝔪^h; there are q^h = |V/𝔪^h| of them.
(c): Σ_{k<n} v(a_n − a_k) = Σ_{k<n} v_q(n − k) = Σ_{l=1}^{n} v_q(l) = w_q(n) (CA.3/legendre-exponent).

(d): v(∏_{k<n}(x − a_k)) = Σ_{h≥1} #{k < n : x ≡ a_k mod 𝔪^h}. Split 0, …, n − 1 into ⌊n/q^h⌋ full blocks of q^h consecutive indices and a remainder; by (b) each full block contains exactly one k with a_k ≡ x mod 𝔪^h. Summing over h gives at least Σ_h ⌊n/q^h⌋ = w_q(n).
The shifted sequence satisfies (a) with the same right-hand side, so (b)–(d) hold for it too (the strong v-ordering property).
acceptance: V = ℤ_(p), π = p, r_i = i: a_n = n for every n, and (c) is Legendre's formula v_p(n!) = w_p(n).

nodes.title: Regular basis and characteristic ideals of Int(V) for a discrete valuation ring
nodes.statement: Let V be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer π. (1) If the residue field of V is finite of cardinality q and (a_n) is the v-ordering of CA.3/v-ordering-of-a-dvr, the polynomials f_n = ∏_{k<n}(X − a_k)/(a_n − a_k) form a regular basis of Int(V); a polynomial of degree at most n lies in Int(V) iff its values at any n + 1 consecutive terms a_s, …, a_{s+n} lie in V; and I_n(V) = π^{−w_q(n)} V. (2) If the residue field of V is infinite, Int(V) = V[X] and I_n(V) = V for every n.
hypotheses: V a discrete valuation ring with fraction field K.
proofSteps: (1): by property (d) of the v-ordering, v(f_n(x)) = v(∏_{k<n}(x − a_k)) − v(∏_{k<n}(a_n − a_k)) ≥ w_q(n) − w_q(n) = 0, so f_n ∈ Int(V).

CA.3/newton-sequence-criterion then gives the regular basis, the test on a_0, …, a_n, and I_n(V) generated by 1/∏_{k<n}(a_n − a_k), of valuation −w_q(n) by property (c). The shifted sequence is again a v-ordering, which gives the test on any n + 1 consecutive terms.

(2): choose x_0, …, x_n ∈ V in pairwise distinct residue classes. For f ∈ Int(V) of degree ≤ n, Lagrange interpolation at the x_i gives d f ∈ V[X] with d = ∏_{i<j}(x_j − x_i) a unit (Cahen–Chabert, Remark 4), so f ∈ V[X].
acceptance: V = ℤ_(p): the binomial polynomials (X choose n) form a regular basis of Int(ℤ_(p)) and I_n(ℤ_(p)) = p^{−v_p(n!)} ℤ_(p).
V = ℤ[i] localized at (1 + i) (q = 2): I_2(V) = π^{−1}V, I_3(V) = π^{−1}V and I_4(V) = π^{−3}V, although 4! = 24 has valuation 6 there.
V = ℂ[[t]] (infinite residue field): Int(V) = V[X].

nodes.title: The local formula for the characteristic ideals of a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: Let D be a Dedekind domain that is not a field and whose residue fields D/𝔪 are all finite, and write N(𝔪) = |D/𝔪|. For every n ≥ 0 and every maximal ideal 𝔪, the exponent of 𝔪 in the fractional ideal I_n(D) is −w_{N(𝔪)}(n); that is, I_n(D) = ∏_𝔪 𝔪^{−w_{N(𝔪)}(n)}. The product is finite: w_{N(𝔪)}(n) = 0 unless N(𝔪) ≤ n, and only finitely many maximal ideals have norm at most n.
hypotheses: D a Dedekind domain, not a field (so D is infinite), with every residue field finite; the main case is D = 𝓞_K for a number field K, where N(𝔪) is the absolute norm.
proofSteps: I_n(D) is a nonzero fractional ideal containing 1 (CA.3/characteristic-ideals-of-int).

Finiteness: for any n + 1 distinct elements a_0, …, a_n of D, every maximal ideal of norm at most n contains d = ∏_{i<j}(a_j − a_i) ≠ 0 (two of the a_i are congruent modulo it), so only finitely many have norm ≤ n.
Localization (CA.3/int-valued-localization (iii), D Noetherian): I_n(D)_𝔪 = I_n(D_𝔪).

D_𝔪 is a discrete valuation ring with residue field D/𝔪 (Mathlib IsLocalization.AtPrime.isDiscreteValuationRing_of_dedekind_domain), so I_n(D_𝔪) = 𝔪^{−w_{N(𝔪)}(n)} D_𝔪 by CA.3/local-regular-basis-of-int-dvr.

Exponents from localizations: for a nonzero fractional ideal J and a maximal ideal 𝔪, FractionalIdeal.count 𝔪 J is the 𝔪-adic valuation of a generator of the principal fractional ideal J D_𝔪, because count is additive on products (FractionalIdeal.count_mul), equals 1 on 𝔪 (count_self) and 0 on every other maximal ideal (count_maximal_coprime), and those other maximal ideals become the unit ideal in D_𝔪. Hence count 𝔪 I_n(D) = −w_{N(𝔪)}(n) by the previous step, and FractionalIdeal.finprod_heightOneSpectrum_factorization' writes I_n(D) as the product of the maximal ideals to these exponents.
acceptance: D = ℤ: I_n(ℤ) = ∏_p p^{−v_p(n!)} ℤ = (1/n!) ℤ, agreeing with CA.3/characteristic-ideals-of-int.
D = 𝓞_K for K = ℚ(√−5): I_2(D) = 𝔭_2^{−1} with 𝔭_2 = (2, 1 + √−5), a non-principal fractional ideal.

nodes.title: The factorial ideals n!_D of a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: Let D be a Dedekind domain whose residue fields are all finite, with N(𝔪) = |D/𝔪|. The n-th factorial ideal of D is the integral ideal n!_D = ∏_𝔪 𝔪^{w_{N(𝔪)}(n)} (a finite product). When D is not a field it is the inverse of the n-th characteristic ideal: n!_D = I_n(D)⁻¹ (CA.3/characteristic-ideals-of-a-dedekind-domain). This is Bhargava's factorial of the subset D of D.
hypotheses: D a Dedekind domain with finite residue fields; the main case is D = 𝓞_K.
proofSteps: Define n!_D as the finite product over the maximal ideals of norm at most n of 𝔪^{w_{N(𝔪)}(n)} (the other factors are D).
Identification with I_n(D)⁻¹ when D is not a field: compare exponents with CA.3/characteristic-ideals-of-a-dedekind-domain.
Product formula: n!_D = ∏_q Π_q(D)^{w_q(n)}, grouping the maximal ideals by their norm q (CA.3/polya-ideal).
Divisibility m!_D · n!_D | (m + n)!_D from w_q(m) + w_q(n) ≤ w_q(m + n), and n!_D | (n + 1)!_D from monotonicity of w_q.
D = ℤ: n!_ℤ = ∏_p p^{v_p(n!)} ℤ = n! ℤ by Legendre's formula.
acceptance: n!_ℤ = n!·ℤ.
4!_{ℤ[i]} = (1 + i)³, of norm 8, while 4!·ℤ[i] has norm 576.
2!_{𝓞_K} = 𝔭_2 = (2, 1 + √−5) for K = ℚ(√−5), which is not principal.

nodes.title: The ideals Π_q(D): product of the primes of norm q
nodes.statement: Let D be a Dedekind domain whose residue fields are finite. For an integer q ≥ 2, Π_q(D) is the product of the maximal ideals 𝔪 of D with N(𝔪) = q; it is the unit ideal D when no maximal ideal has norm q (for example when q is not a prime power). For D = 𝓞_K only finitely many maximal ideals have a given norm, so the product is finite.
hypotheses: D a Dedekind domain with finite residue fields such that each norm is attained by finitely many maximal ideals (true for 𝓞_K and for any D that is not a field, by the pigeonhole argument of CA.3/characteristic-ideals-of-a-dedekind-domain).
proofSteps: Define Π_q(D) as the finite product of the maximal ideals of norm q.
Its exponent at 𝔪 is 1 if N(𝔪) = q and 0 otherwise; hence Π_q and Π_{q′} are coprime for q ≠ q′.
If q is not a prime power, no residue field has q elements and Π_q(D) = D.
Galois case (CA.3/polya-group-of-a-galois-field): Π_{p^f}(𝓞_K)^e = p𝓞_K, where e and f are the common ramification index and residue degree of p.
acceptance: Π_p(ℤ) = pℤ and Π_4(ℤ) = ℤ.

nodes.title: Factorial ideals and the ideals Π_q generate the same free group
nodes.statement: Let D be a Dedekind domain, not a field, with finite residue fields. In the group of nonzero fractional ideals of D, the subgroup generated by the factorial ideals n!_D (n ≥ 0) — equivalently by the characteristic ideals I_n(D) — equals the subgroup generated by the ideals Π_q(D) (q ≥ 2), and the Π_q(D) different from D form a basis of this free abelian group. Explicitly n!_D = ∏_q Π_q(D)^{w_q(n)}, n!_D · ((n − 1)!_D)⁻¹ = ∏_q Π_q(D)^{v_q(n)} for n ≥ 1, and for a prime power q = p^f: Π_q(D) = q!_D · ((q − 1)!_D)⁻¹ · ∏_{1≤j<f} Π_{p^j}(D)^{−⌊f/j⌋}.
hypotheses: D a Dedekind domain, not a field, with finite residue fields.
proofSteps: n!_D = ∏_q Π_q(D)^{w_q(n)}: group the maximal ideals by their norm in CA.3/factorial-ideal.
Quotients: w_q(n) − w_q(n − 1) = v_q(n) (CA.3/legendre-exponent), giving the second formula.

For n = p^f: v_q(p^f) = ⌊f/j⌋ if q = p^j (1 ≤ j ≤ f) and 0 for every other q, so q!_D/(q − 1)!_D = ∏_{j≤f} Π_{p^j}(D)^{⌊f/j⌋}, in which Π_{p^f} has exponent 1. Induction on f expresses each Π_{p^f}(D) through factorial ideals, so the two subgroups coincide.
Freeness: distinct Π_q have disjoint sets of prime factors, so ∏_q Π_q(D)^{c_q} = D forces c_q = 0 whenever Π_q(D) ≠ D, by unique factorization of fractional ideals (Mathlib FractionalIdeal.count).
acceptance: D = ℤ: the factorial group is free on the pℤ; for q = 4: Π_4(ℤ) = (4!/3!)ℤ · (2ℤ)^{−2} = ℤ, as it must.

nodes.title: The Pólya–Ostrowski criterion for regular bases of Int(D)
nodes.statement: Let D be a Dedekind domain, not a field, with finite residue fields (for example D = 𝓞_K for a number field K). The following are equivalent: (i) the D-module Int(D) has a regular basis; (ii) every characteristic ideal I_n(D) is principal; (iii) every factorial ideal n!_D is principal; (iv) every ideal Π_q(D), q ≥ 2, is principal. When they hold and n!_D = d_n D, any choice of f_n ∈ Int(D) of degree n with leading coefficient 1/d_n is a regular basis.
hypotheses: D a Dedekind domain, not a field, with finite residue fields; D is then infinite, as the regular-basis criterion requires.
proofSteps: (i) ⇔ (ii) and the description of regular bases: CA.3/regular-basis-iff-characteristic-ideals-principal.
(ii) ⇔ (iii): I_n(D) = (n!_D)⁻¹ (CA.3/factorial-ideal), and a nonzero fractional ideal is principal iff its inverse is.

(iii) ⇔ (iv): the principal fractional ideals form a subgroup, and by CA.3/factorial-group-basis the factorial ideals and the Π_q generate the same subgroup; each family lies in the principal subgroup iff the other does.
acceptance: D = ℤ: all four hold; the binomial polynomials are the regular basis.
K = ℚ(√−5): (iii) fails at n = 2 (2!_{𝓞_K} = 𝔭_2), so Int(𝓞_K) has no regular basis.
K = ℚ(√−23): every Π_q(𝓞_K) is principal (the only ramified prime gives Π_23 = (√−23)), so Int(𝓞_K) has a regular basis although 𝓞_K is not a principal ideal domain (class number 3).
Every principal ideal domain D with finite residue fields satisfies (i).

nodes.title: Pólya fields
nodes.statement: A number field K is a Pólya field if the 𝓞_K-module Int(𝓞_K) has a regular basis, i.e. a basis (f_n)_{n≥0} with deg f_n = n. By CA.3/polya-ostrowski-criterion this holds iff every factorial ideal n!_{𝓞_K} is principal, iff every Π_q(𝓞_K) is principal, iff the Pólya group Po(K) is trivial.
hypotheses: K a number field with ring of integers 𝓞_K.
proofSteps: Define IsPolyaField K as the existence of a regular basis of Int(𝓞_K) (a Module.Basis ℕ 𝓞_K Int(𝓞_K) whose n-th vector has degree n).
Equivalences: CA.3/polya-ostrowski-criterion and CA.3/polya-group.
Class number one implies Pólya: every Π_q is principal.
ℚ is a Pólya field (the binomial polynomials, CA.3/polya-binomial-basis).
acceptance: ℚ and ℚ(i) are Pólya fields; ℚ(√−5) is not; ℚ(√−23) is, with class number 3.

nodes.title: The Pólya group of a number field
nodes.statement: For a number field K, the Pólya group Po(K) is the subgroup of the class group Cl(K) = ClassGroup(𝓞_K) generated by the classes of the factorial ideals n!_{𝓞_K}, n ≥ 0. By CA.3/factorial-group-basis it is also generated by the classes of the ideals Π_q(𝓞_K), q ≥ 2; it is the image in Cl(K) of the factorial group, and K is a Pólya field iff Po(K) is trivial.
hypotheses: K a number field.
proofSteps: Define Po(K) as the subgroup closure of {[n!_{𝓞_K}] : n ≥ 0} in ClassGroup(𝓞_K) (each n!_{𝓞_K} is a nonzero ideal, so its class is ClassGroup.mk0).
Equality with the closure of the classes [Π_q(𝓞_K)]: the two families generate the same subgroup of ideals (CA.3/factorial-group-basis), and the class map is a homomorphism.
Po(K) = ⊥ iff every [n!_{𝓞_K}] is trivial iff every n!_{𝓞_K} is principal (Mathlib ClassGroup.mk0_eq_one_iff), iff K is a Pólya field (CA.3/polya-ostrowski-criterion).
Po(K) ≤ Cl(K), so |Po(K)| divides the class number.

nodes.title: Ostrowski's theorem: the Pólya group of a Galois number field
nodes.statement: Let K/ℚ be a finite Galois extension, and for a prime p let e_p and f_p be the common ramification index and residue degree of the primes of 𝓞_K above p. Then Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K)^{e_p} = p𝓞_K and Π_{p^j}(𝓞_K) = 𝓞_K for j ≠ f_p. Consequently Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K) is principal whenever p is unramified, Po(K) is generated by the classes of Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K) for the finitely many ramified primes p, each of order dividing e_p, and |Po(K)| divides ∏_{p ramified} e_p. In particular, if [K : ℚ] is coprime to the class number of K, then K is a Pólya field.
hypotheses: K/ℚ finite Galois.
proofSteps: All primes 𝔓 above p have the same ramification index and residue degree (Mathlib Ideal.ramificationIdx_eq_of_isGaloisGroup and Ideal.inertiaDeg_eq_of_isGaloisGroup), so they all have norm p^{f_p} (Mathlib Ideal.natAbs_pow_inertiaDeg, stated with the same inertia degree as the Galois lemma), and no other prime of 𝓞_K has a norm that is a power of p.
p𝓞_K = ∏_{𝔓 | p} 𝔓^{e_p} (Ideal.IsDedekindDomain.ramificationIdx_eq_normalizedFactors_count with Ideal.prod_normalizedFactors_eq_self) = Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K)^{e_p}.

For unramified p (e_p = 1), Π_{p^{f_p}} = p𝓞_K is principal. By CA.3/polya-group, Po(K) is generated by the classes [Π_q]; only q = p^{f_p} with p ramified can contribute, and [Π_{p^{f_p}}]^{e_p} = [p𝓞_K] = 1.
A finite abelian group generated by elements whose orders divide e_{p_1}, …, e_{p_s} has order dividing ∏ e_{p_i}.
Coprime degree: each e_p divides [K : ℚ] = e_p f_p g_p, so every prime factor of |Po(K)| divides [K : ℚ]; since |Po(K)| also divides the class number, coprimality forces |Po(K)| = 1.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√−5): ramified primes 2 and 5; Π_2 = (2, 1 + √−5) is not principal and Π_5 = (√−5) is, so Po(K) ≅ ℤ/2.
K = ℚ(√−23): only 23 ramifies and Π_23 = (√−23), so Po(K) = 1 while the class number is 3.
K = ℚ(i): Π_2 = (1 + i), so K is a Pólya field.

nodes.title: The imaginary quadratic Pólya fields
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(√d) with d < 0 squarefree and discriminant D_K (D_K = d if d ≡ 1 mod 4, D_K = 4d otherwise). Then Po(K) is generated by the classes of the ramified prime ideals 𝔭 (𝔭² = p𝓞_K for p | D_K), and it is nontrivial as soon as at least two primes ramify. Hence K is a Pólya field iff exactly one prime ramifies in K, iff d = −1, d = −2, or d = −p for a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
hypotheses: d < 0 squarefree, K = ℚ(√d); the primes ramified in K are the primes dividing D_K.
proofSteps: By CA.3/polya-group-of-a-galois-field (K/ℚ is Galois of degree 2), Po(K) is generated by the classes of the Π_p = 𝔭 for ramified p (f = 1, e = 2).

Ring of integers: 𝓞_K = ℤ[√d] for d ≢ 1 (mod 4) and ℤ[(1 + √d)/2] for d ≡ 1 (mod 4) (CA.5/index-of-the-order-z-sqrt-d). The norm of x = a + bω is a² + |d|b² ≥ |D_K|/4, respectively (a + b/2)² + |D_K|b²/4 ≥ |D_K|/4, whenever b ≠ 0.

Two or more ramified primes: let p_1 be the smallest. If D_K ≡ 0 (mod 4) then p_1 = 2 and |D_K|/4 = |d| ≥ 3 because d has an odd prime factor; if D_K ≡ 1 (mod 4) then |D_K| ≥ p_1 p_2 > 4 p_1. So p_1 < |D_K|/4. A principal ideal of norm p_1 would have a generator of norm p_1 < |D_K|/4, hence a rational integer, whose norm is a square — impossible. So [𝔭_{p_1}] ≠ 1 and Po(K) ≠ 1.

Exactly one ramified prime: then D_K ∈ {−4, −8} or D_K = −p with p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (an odd discriminant d ≡ 1 mod 4 with one prime factor), and the ramified prime ideal is (1 + i), (√−2) or (√−p) respectively, which is principal; so Po(K) = 1.
The list: D_K = −4 ⇔ d = −1, D_K = −8 ⇔ d = −2, D_K = −p ⇔ d = −p with p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
acceptance: ℚ(i), ℚ(√−2), ℚ(√−3), ℚ(√−7), ℚ(√−23) are Pólya fields; ℚ(√−23) has class number 3.
ℚ(√−5) (D_K = −20) and ℚ(√−15) (D_K = −15) are not: in ℚ(√−15) the prime 𝔭_3 above 3 is not principal since 3 < 15/4.
ℚ(√−6) (D_K = −24, ramified 2 and 3): 𝔭_2 is not principal since 2 < 6.

nodes.title: Zantema's theorem: cyclotomic fields are Pólya fields
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1 the cyclotomic field K = ℚ(ζ_n) is a Pólya field. Explicitly, for a prime p write n = p^k m with p ∤ m and let f_p be the order of p modulo m. Then Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K) = p𝓞_K if k = 0 and Π_{p^{f_p}}(𝓞_K) = (1 − ζ_n^{m})𝓞_K if k ≥ 1 (ζ_n^m is a primitive p^k-th root of unity), every other Π_q(𝓞_K) is 𝓞_K, and so N!_{𝓞_K} is generated by ∏_{p ∤ n} p^{w_{p^{f_p}}(N)} · ∏_{p | n} (1 − ζ_n^{n/p^{v_p(n)}})^{w_{p^{f_p}}(N)} for every N.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1, K = ℚ(ζ_n) a cyclotomic extension of ℚ.
proofSteps: K/ℚ is Galois (Mathlib IsCyclotomicExtension.isGalois), so CA.3/polya-group-of-a-galois-field applies: for p ∤ n, p is unramified (IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.ramificationIdxIn_eq_of_not_dvd) and Π_{p^{f_p}} = p𝓞_K.
For p | n with n = p^k m, k ≥ 1: e_p = p^{k−1}(p − 1) (IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.ramificationIdxIn_eq), so p𝓞_K = Π_{p^{f_p}}^{e_p}.

In the subfield L = ℚ(ζ) with ζ = ζ_n^m of order p^k, the unique prime above p is (1 − ζ)𝓞_L (IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.eq_span_zeta_sub_one_of_liesOver) with ramification index p^{k−1}(p − 1) (ramificationIdxIn_eq_of_prime_pow), so p𝓞_L = ((1 − ζ)𝓞_L)^{e_p}.
Extending to 𝓞_K: ((1 − ζ)𝓞_K)^{e_p} = p𝓞_K = Π_{p^{f_p}}^{e_p}; unique factorization of ideals gives (1 − ζ)𝓞_K = Π_{p^{f_p}}.

All Π_q are principal, so K is a Pólya field by CA.3/polya-ostrowski-criterion, and the generator of N!_{𝓞_K} follows from the product formula N!_{𝓞_K} = ∏_q Π_q(𝓞_K)^{w_q(N)} of CA.3/factorial-ideal.
acceptance: ℚ(ζ_23) is a Pólya field although its class number is 3.

nodes.title: Mignotte's inequality for irreducible integer factors
nodes.statement: Let A ∈ ℤ[X] be nonzero and let I ∈ ℤ[X] be an irreducible factor of A of degree m ≥ 1. Then ‖I‖₂ ≤ e^{√m} (m + 2√m + 2)^{1+√m} ‖A‖₂^{1+√m}, where ‖·‖₂ is the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector. This is the form in which Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma quote Mignotte (1988), Theorem 1′ and the remarks after it.
hypotheses: A ∈ ℤ[X], A ≠ 0; I ∈ ℤ[X] irreducible, I | A, deg I = m ≥ 1. Whether Mignotte's Theorem 1′ needs further hypotheses (for example on the leading coefficient or on the multiplicity of I in A) has not been checked against the source (see gaps).
proofSteps: Source of record: Mignotte, An inequality about irreducible factors of integer polynomials, J. Number Theory 30 (1988), 156–166, Theorem 1′ and the remarks below it, as cited in Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma, proof of Lemma 3.4. That paper was not readable here (the publisher refuses automated access), so its proof is not decomposed; this is recorded as a gap.

What the pinned library gives, and why it does not suffice: write A = I·J with J ∈ ℤ[X]; M(J) ≥ |lc(J)| ≥ 1, so M(I) ≤ M(A) (Mathlib mahlerMeasure_mul), and M(A) ≤ ‖A‖₂ (Landau, mahlerMeasure_le_sqrt_sum_sq_norm_coeff). With |coeff_k(I)| ≤ C(m, k) M(I) (norm_coeff_le_choose_mul_mahlerMeasure) this yields the classical bound ‖I‖₂ ≤ C(2m, m)^{1/2} ‖A‖₂, whose factor grows like 2^m; the statement here replaces it by a factor (m‖A‖₂)^{O(√m)}, which is smaller once m is large compared with (log ‖A‖₂)², and no combination of the library bounds gives that.
acceptance: When A = I is itself irreducible the inequality is immediate, since e^{√m}(m + 2√m + 2)^{1+√m}‖I‖₂^{√m} ≥ 1.
The classical consequence ‖I‖₂ ≤ C(2m, m)^{1/2}‖A‖₂ holds for every factor (irreducible or not), e.g. A = (X + 1)^m, I = A: ‖I‖₂² = C(2m, m).

sources.match: The proof quotes this inequality for an irreducible integer factor I of degree m of A, citing Mignotte's Theorem 1′ and the remarks below it.

nodes.title: Size of an irreducible factor at an integer point
nodes.statement: Let A ∈ ℤ[X] have degree n ≥ 1 with every coefficient in [−H, H] for some H ≥ 1, and let I ∈ ℤ[X] be irreducible in ℤ[X] of degree m ≥ 0 with I | A (for m = 0, I = ±p for a prime p). Then for every integer N ≥ 2, |I(N)| ≤ N^m · exp(4(1 + √m) log(14√n H)).
hypotheses: A ∈ ℤ[X] of degree n ≥ 1 with all coefficients bounded by H ≥ 1; I an irreducible element of ℤ[X] dividing A, of degree m ≥ 0 (so m ≤ n; the source allows any irreducible polynomial over ℤ, which includes the prime constants); N ≥ 2 an integer.
proofSteps: m = 0: I = ±p for a prime p dividing every coefficient of A; the leading coefficient of A is nonzero, so p ≤ H ≤ (14√n H)⁴ = exp(4 log(14√n H)), which is the bound with N⁰ = 1. The remaining steps treat m ≥ 1.
‖A‖₂ ≤ H√(n + 1), since A has n + 1 coefficients (the source prints H√n; the correction is recorded as PAPER-BARYSOROKER-KOUKOULOPOULOS-KOZMA-23/E15 and does not affect the conclusion).
Cauchy–Schwarz (Mathlib Finset.sum_mul_sq_le_sq_mul_sq) applied to I(N) = Σ_{i≤m} c_i N^i: |I(N)| ≤ (Σ_{i≤m} N^{2i})^{1/2} ‖I‖₂ ≤ N^m (N²/(N² − 1))^{1/2} ‖I‖₂ ≤ (2/√3) N^m ‖I‖₂.
CA.3/mignotte-irreducible-factor-l2-bound: ‖I‖₂ ≤ e^{√m}(m + 2√m + 2)^{1+√m}(H√(n + 1))^{1+√m}.

Arithmetic with m ≤ n and n ≥ 1: e^{√m} ≤ e^{1+√m}, m + 2√m + 2 ≤ 5n and √(n + 1) ≤ √2·√n, so ‖I‖₂ ≤ (5√2 e · n^{3/2} H)^{1+√m}; as (2/√3)·5√2e < 23 < 14⁴ and n^{3/2}H ≤ n²H⁴, the product is at most (14⁴ n² H⁴)^{1+√m} = exp(4(1 + √m) log(14√n H)).
acceptance: The bound is used with a prime p > p_0 dividing A(N): p divides some irreducible factor's value, forcing that factor to have degree > (1 − θ)n (Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma, proof of Lemma 3.3, p. 21).
With the corrected ‖A‖₂ ≤ H√(n + 1) the printed final inequality still holds, with room to spare.
Constant factor: A = 2X + 2, I = 2 (irreducible in ℤ[X]), n = 1, H = 2, m = 0: |I(N)| = 2 ≤ (14·2)⁴.

sources.match: The statement is Lemma 3.4; the proof combines the quoted Mignotte inequality with the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate for |I(N)| as above. The lemma is stated for any irreducible I over ℤ; the constant case m = 0, which the proof does not mention, is the first step above.

nodes.title: The primitive gcd of a family of integer polynomials
nodes.statement: Let Q_1, …, Q_k (k ≥ 1) be nonzero polynomials in ℤ[X]. Their primitive gcd G = gcd(Q_1, …, Q_k) is the unique primitive polynomial G ∈ ℤ[X] with positive leading coefficient that generates, in ℚ[X], the same ideal as the monic gcd of the Q_i (equivalently, G is of maximal degree among primitive integer polynomials dividing every Q_i in ℚ[X]). By Gauss's lemma G divides each Q_i in ℤ[X], and the quotients Q_i/G ∈ ℤ[X] have no common nonconstant factor in ℚ[X].
hypotheses: Q_1, …, Q_k nonzero, k ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Let g ∈ ℚ[X] be the monic gcd of the images of the Q_i (Mathlib Finset.gcd in ℚ[X]); clear denominators and take the primitive part (Mathlib Polynomial.primPart), adjusting the sign so that the leading coefficient is positive.
Uniqueness: two primitive integer polynomials that are associate in ℚ[X] differ by a rational unit that must be ±1, and the sign is fixed by the leading coefficient.
Divisibility in ℤ[X]: G is primitive and divides Q_i in ℚ[X], so it divides Q_i in ℤ[X] (Mathlib Polynomial.IsPrimitive.dvd_iff_fraction_map_dvd_fraction_map).
Maximality: a primitive H dividing every Q_i in ℚ[X] divides g, hence G, in ℚ[X], hence in ℤ[X].
acceptance: gcd(2X, 4X) = X, whereas the gcd of 2X and 4X in the GCD monoid ℤ[X] is 2X.
gcd(X² − 1, X² + X) = X + 1; gcd(−6X − 4) = 3X + 2.

nodes.title: A bounded squarefree integral combination of integer polynomials
nodes.statement: Let k ≥ 1, n ≥ 0 and let Q_1, …, Q_k ∈ ℤ[X] be nonzero of degree at most n, with some Q_i of degree exactly n; let G be their primitive gcd (CA.3/primitive-polynomial-gcd) and d = n − deg G. Then there are integers b_2, …, b_k ≥ 0 with b_2 + ⋯ + b_k ≤ max(2d − 1, 0) (so each b_j ≤ 2d) such that Q = (Q_1 + b_2Q_2 + ⋯ + b_kQ_k)/G lies in ℤ[X], has degree exactly d, and is squarefree in ℚ[X] (it has no repeated complex root). The integer content of Q need not be squarefree.
hypotheses: Q_1, …, Q_k nonzero in ℤ[X], all of degree ≤ n, at least one of degree n.
proofSteps: d = 0: take every b_j = 0; Q = Q_1/G is a nonzero constant, hence of degree 0 and squarefree in ℚ[X].
d > 0: let F = Q_1/G + x_2·Q_2/G + ⋯ + x_k·Q_k/G ∈ ℤ[x_2, …, x_k][t]. Its t-degree is d with leading coefficient ℓ = Σ_j c_j x_j (x_1 = 1, c_j the coefficient of t^d in Q_j/G), and ℓ ≠ 0.

F is irreducible over the field ℚ(x_2, …, x_k): F has degree 1 in the x-variables, so in a factorization F = F_1F_2 over ℚ[x][t] one factor lies in ℚ[t] and divides every Q_j/G, hence is constant (primitive gcd); Gauss's lemma passes to ℚ(x)[t].

Let R = Res_{d, d−1}(F, ∂F/∂t) ∈ ℤ[x], the Sylvester determinant with formal degrees d and d − 1 (Mathlib Polynomial.resultant with explicit sizes). Its entries have x-degree ≤ 1, so total degree R ≤ 2d − 1. Over ℚ(x), F is irreducible of positive degree in characteristic 0, hence coprime to its nonzero derivative, and its leading coefficient is nonzero; so R ≠ 0 (Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff over a field, transported by resultant_map_map along ℤ[x] → ℚ(x)).

Specialization: for b ∈ ℤ^{k−1}, R(b) = Res_{d, d−1}(F(b), F(b)′) (resultant_map_map with evaluation at b). If deg F(b) < d then also deg F(b)′ < d − 1 and R(b) = 0 (resultant_eq_zero_of_lt_lt). So R(b) ≠ 0 forces deg F(b) = d and F(b) coprime to F(b)′ in ℚ[t], i.e. F(b) separable, hence squarefree (Polynomial.Separable.squarefree).

Grid point: pick a monomial x^τ of degree totalDegree R with nonzero coefficient in R; the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz (Mathlib MvPolynomial.combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_eval_nonzero) with S_j = {0, 1, …, τ_j} gives b with 0 ≤ b_j ≤ τ_j and R(b) ≠ 0, so Σ b_j ≤ Σ τ_j ≤ 2d − 1. Smith instead invokes Salzer's multivariate Gregory–Newton formula.
Q = F(b) has integer coefficients because each Q_j/G ∈ ℤ[X], degree d and no repeated root.
acceptance: Q_1 = X², Q_2 = 1 (G = 1, d = 2): b_2 = 0 gives X², which is not squarefree; b_2 = 1 gives X² + 1, which is.
Q_1 = 4X + 4 (k = 1): G = X + 1, d = 0 and Q = 4, a nonzero constant: squarefree in ℚ[X] although its content 4 is not squarefree.

Warning for formalization: the specialization identity in step 5 holds for the Sylvester determinant Res(F, F′) with fixed formal degrees; the normalized discriminant (Mathlib Polynomial.discr, which divides by the leading coefficient and uses the actual degree) does not vanish when the degree drops by one (a t² + b t + c at a = 0 has discriminant b²).

nodes.title: Fujiwara's weighted root bound
nodes.statement: Let f = a_0X^n + a_1X^{n−1} + ⋯ + a_n ∈ ℂ[X] with n ≥ 1 and a_0 ≠ 0, and let λ_1, …, λ_n > 0 satisfy Σ_k 1/λ_k ≤ 1. Then every root α of f satisfies |α| ≤ max_{1≤k≤n} (λ_k |a_k/a_0|)^{1/k}. If Σ_k 1/λ_k < 1 and some a_k (k ≥ 1) is nonzero, the inequality is strict.
proofSteps: Let B = max_k (λ_k|a_k/a_0|)^{1/k} and suppose ρ = |α| > B ≥ 0. For every k, ρ^k > λ_k|a_k/a_0|, so |a_k|ρ^{n−k} < |a_0|ρ^n/λ_k (also when a_k = 0, since ρ > 0).
Summing, Σ_{k≥1}|a_k|ρ^{n−k} < |a_0|ρ^n Σ_k 1/λ_k ≤ |a_0|ρ^n, so |f(α)| ≥ |a_0|ρ^n − Σ_{k≥1}|a_k|ρ^{n−k} > 0 (triangle inequality), a contradiction.

Strict form: if Σ1/λ_k < 1 and ρ = B > 0, the same estimate gives Σ|a_k|ρ^{n−k} ≤ |a_0|ρ^n Σ 1/λ_k < |a_0|ρ^n. When every a_k (k ≥ 1) vanishes, B = 0 and α = 0, so strictness fails; this degenerate case is excluded.
acceptance: λ_k = n gives Cauchy's form |α| ≤ max_k (n|a_k/a_0|)^{1/k} (Fujiwara's (2)).
λ_k = 2^k gives |α| ≤ 2·max_k |a_k/a_0|^{1/k} (Fujiwara's (3)); for f = X² − 4 the bound is 2·2 = 4 ≥ 2.
Mathlib's Cauchy bound (Polynomial.cauchyBound, 1 + max|a_k/a_0|) is a different estimate: for X² − 4 it gives 5.

sources.match: Derives exactly this bound from the lower estimate |f(x)| ≥ |a_0|ρ^n − Σ|a_k|ρ^{n−k} under Σ1/λ_k ≤ 1; the footnote asserts the strict inequality when Σ1/λ_k < 1 (its degenerate case is recorded in sourceIssues).

nodes.title: The Gregory–Newton expansion of a polynomial in binomial polynomials
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and f ∈ K[X] of degree at most N. Then f = Σ_{k=0}^{N} (Δ^k f)(0)·(X choose k) in K[X], where Δg(X) = g(X + 1) − g(X), and (Δ^k f)(0) = Σ_{j=0}^{k} (−1)^{k−j} C(k, j) f(j). Moreover Δ^k f = 0 for k > deg f. In particular, for f ∈ Int(ℤ) every coefficient (Δ^k f)(0) is an integer, and these are the coefficients c_k of Pólya's expansion.
hypotheses: K a field of characteristic 0 (so that (X choose k) ∈ K[X] and polynomials agreeing on ℕ are equal).
proofSteps: Newton's formula (Mathlib shift_eq_sum_fwdDiff_iter with step 1 at 0): f(n) = Σ_{k≤n} C(n, k)(Δ^k f)(0) for every n ∈ ℕ.
Δ lowers the degree by one, so Δ^k f = 0 for k > deg f; hence for all n the right side is Σ_{k≤N} (Δ^k f)(0)·(n choose k).
Both sides are polynomials agreeing at every natural number, an infinite set, so they are equal (Mathlib Polynomial.eq_of_infinite_eval_eq).
The finite-difference formula is Mathlib fwdDiff_iter_eq_sum_shift; for f ∈ Int(ℤ) it is an integer combination of integers.
acceptance: f = X²: (Δf)(0) = 1, (Δ²f)(0) = 2, so X² = (X choose 1) + 2·(X choose 2).
f = X(X − 1)/2: the coefficients are 0, 0, 1.

Compatibility: the coefficients (Δ^k f)(0) are the coordinates of f in Tau Ceti's basis TauCeti.binomialPolynomialBasis of K[X] (a field of characteristic 0 is a ℚ-algebra), which also gives their uniqueness.

nodes.title: The lower Newton polygon of a finite point family
nodes.statement: Let I ⊂ ℕ be a nonempty finite set and y : I → ℝ (the points (i, y_i)). For r ∈ ℝ put μ_r = min_{i∈I}(y_i + r·i), the contact set C_r = {i ∈ I : y_i + r·i = μ_r}, ℓ_r = min C_r, u_r = max C_r and the width m_r = u_r − ℓ_r. Orientation (as in CA.3/newton-slope-multiplicity): in the plane of the points (−i, y_i) the line of slope r through (−i, y_i) has intercept y_i + r·i, so μ_r is the intercept of the supporting line of slope r and the lower convex hull of these points (the Newton polygon) has a side of slope r exactly when m_r > 0, joining the points of abscissae −u_r and −ℓ_r; in the plane of the points (i, y_i) the same side has geometric slope −r. Then: (a) y_i + r·i ≥ μ_r for all i ∈ I, with equality exactly on C_r (every point lies on or above the supporting line, and the points on it are the contact set); (b) only finitely many r have m_r > 0; (c) Σ_r m_r = max I − min I; (d) slope ordering: if r < r′ then u_{r′} ≤ ℓ_r; (e) y_{u_r} = y_{ℓ_r} − r·m_r; (f) r ↦ μ_r is concave and piecewise affine. For a nonzero f = Σ a_iX^i over a field with valuation v, I = supp f and y_i = v(a_i) give μ_r = v_r(f) (CA.3/sloped-valuation) and m_r = m_r(f) (CA.3/newton-slope-multiplicity).
hypotheses: I ⊂ ℕ finite and nonempty; y : I → ℝ. (Points with y_i = ∞, such as zero coefficients, are left out of I.)
proofSteps: μ_r is a minimum over a finite nonempty set (Mathlib Finset.inf' over I), C_r is nonempty, and (a) is the definition.
(d): for i ∈ C_{r′} and j ∈ C_r, y_i + r′i ≤ y_j + r′j and y_j + rj ≤ y_i + ri; adding, (r′ − r)(i − j) ≤ 0, so i ≤ j.

(b) and (c): by (d) the contact intervals [ℓ_r, u_r] of the r with m_r > 0 are ordered decreasingly in r and overlap only at endpoints; such r is the slope (y_j − y_i)/(i − j) of a pair i < j in I, so there are finitely many. For r larger than every such slope C_r = {min I}, for r smaller C_r = {max I}, and as r decreases through the finitely many critical values the contact interval moves from min I to max I, its widths adding to max I − min I.
(e): ℓ_r and u_r both lie on the supporting line.
(f): μ is the minimum of finitely many affine functions of r.

Polynomial case: with y_i = v(a_i) on supp f, μ_r and C_r are those of the sloped valuation and m_r is the slope multiplicity of CA.3/sloped-valuation and CA.3/newton-slope-multiplicity; those polynomial nodes are the specialization of this one (they cite it), so this node does not depend on them.

nodes.title: Gauss–Jordan elimination: the change-of-basis certificate and uniqueness of the reduced form
nodes.statement: Let F be a field with decidable equality and A an m × n matrix over F. Tau Ceti's TauCeti.rowReduce (List.ofFn A) is the terminating Gauss–Jordan sweep (structural recursion over the columns): it returns the nonzero rows of the reduced row echelon form of A, each with its pivot column, and Tau Ceti proves that the matrix TauCeti.rowReduceMatrix they form is in reduced row echelon form with those pivots, that its rows span the row space of A, that there are rank A of them, and that it has the same kernel as A. This node adds what a normal form needs beyond that. (a) Certificate: let R be the m × n matrix formed by the rows of TauCeti.rowReduceMatrix (List.ofFn A) followed by m − rank A zero rows, with pivot function ℓ equal to the recorded pivot columns and then ⊤; there is an invertible m × m matrix P, with an explicit inverse P′ (P P′ = P′ P = 1), such that P A = R, both computed by the same sweep. (b) Uniqueness: two matrices in reduced row echelon form that differ by an invertible left factor are equal; so R, its pivot columns and its free columns depend only on the row-equivalence class of A.
hypotheses: F a field with decidable equality (for example ZMod p, p prime, or ℚ); A an m × n matrix over F. Tau Ceti's sweep works over a division ring; the rank statements use a field.
proofSteps: Sweep, reduced form, pivots, row space, rank and kernel: Tau Ceti TauCeti.rowReduce with isReducedRowEchelon_rowReduceMatrix, isPivotedBy_rowReduceMatrix, span_rowReduce, length_rowReduce_ofFn and mulVec_eq_zero_iff_rowReduceMatrix. Appending zero rows below keeps the reduced row echelon form, with pivot ⊤ on the new rows.

Certificate: apply the sweep to the m × (n + m) augmented matrix [A | 1_m], of rank m. Its m reduced rows span its row space (span_rowReduce), so the reduced matrix is E·[A | 1_m] = [E A | E] for some m × m matrix E, and E has rank m (length_rowReduce_ofFn), hence is invertible. Put P = E.

The left block E A is in reduced row echelon form: the rows whose pivot lies among the first n columns come first and keep the reduced pattern there, and every other row is zero on the first n columns because its leading entry lies to the right of them. By uniqueness (next step) E A = R. The inverse P′ is read off in the same way from the reduced form of [P | 1_m], which is [1_m | P⁻¹].

Uniqueness: if R₁ and R₂ = Q R₁ are in reduced row echelon form with Q invertible, they are row equivalent, and Hefferon, Theorem One.III.2.6 (Yuster's induction on the number of columns, using that row-equivalent matrices have the same homogeneous solution sets, Theorem One.I.1.5 and Lemma One.III.1.5) gives R₁ = R₂.

Rank: R is pivoted by ℓ, so rank R is the number of pivots (Mathlib Matrix.IsPivotedBy.rank_eq); it is rank A by Tau Ceti length_rowReduce_ofFn, and also by Mathlib Matrix.rank_mul_eq_right_of_isUnit_det since P is invertible. Kernel: ker A = ker R because P is invertible, as Tau Ceti mulVec_eq_zero_iff_rowReduceMatrix also shows.
acceptance: Over ℚ: [[1, 2, 1], [2, 4, 0]] reduces to R = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 0, 1]] with pivot columns 0 and 2 and rank 2; as A has full row rank the certificate is unique: P = [[0, 1/2], [1, −1/2]] and P′ = [[1, 1], [2, 0]], and P′ R = A.
Over ZMod 2: [[1, 1], [1, 1]] reduces to [[1, 1], [0, 0]], rank 1: TauCeti.rowReduce returns the single row (1, 1) with pivot 0, and R appends one zero row.
An invertible square A reduces to the identity with P = A⁻¹; A = 0 gives R = 0, no pivots and P = 1.

These give uniqueness (b); the sweep itself is Tau Ceti's. The book works over ℝ; the arguments are field-independent.

nodes.title: The kernel basis of a matrix and of a linear map in chosen bases
nodes.statement: Let F be a field with decidable equality. For an m × n matrix A over F, Tau Ceti reads a basis of ker A off TauCeti.rowReduce: for a free column j (TauCeti.IsFreeColumn, a column with no pivot) the kernel vector β_j = TauCeti.kernelVector (List.ofFn A) j has entry 1 at j, 0 at the other free columns and, at the pivot column of each reduced row, the negated entry of that row in column j; the β_j of the free columns form the basis TauCeti.freeColumnBasis A of ker A, the computable list TauCeti.kernelBasis A lists them (sound, spanning, independent, without repetition), and there are n − rank A of them. This node transports that basis to linear maps: for finite-dimensional F-vector spaces V and W with bases b indexed by Fin n and b′ indexed by Fin m, a linear map φ : V → W and A = LinearMap.toMatrix b b′ φ, a vector x lies in ker φ iff A·(b.repr x) = 0, and the vectors Σ_k (β_j)_k b_k, j a free column of A, form a basis of ker φ; so dim ker φ = n − rank A.
hypotheses: F a field with decidable equality (ZMod p in the main use); V and W finite-dimensional over F with bases indexed by Fin n and Fin m.
proofSteps: Matrix case: Tau Ceti TauCeti.freeColumnBasis with coe_freeColumnBasis_apply, and for the list TauCeti.kernelBasis the theorems mulVec_eq_zero_of_mem_kernelBasis (soundness), span_kernelBasis (completeness), linearIndepOn_kernelBasis and nodup_kernelBasis (independence) and length_kernelBasis and finrank_ker_mulVecLin (the count n − rank A). Their proofs are the classical ones: a reduced row is 1 at its own pivot column and 0 at the others, so it annihilates each β_j; a kernel vector x equals Σ_j x_j β_j over the free columns, because the difference vanishes at the free columns and therefore at the pivot columns; and the β_j restrict to the standard basis on the free columns.
Coordinates: Mathlib LinearMap.toMatrix_mulVec_repr gives A·(b.repr x) = b′.repr (φ x), and b′.repr is injective, so x ∈ ker φ iff b.repr x ∈ ker A.

Transport: the coordinate isomorphism Module.Basis.equivFun b : V ≃ F^n therefore restricts to an isomorphism from ker φ onto LinearMap.ker A.mulVecLin; its inverse sends β_j to Σ_k (β_j)_k b_k (Basis.equivFun_symm_apply), and the image of TauCeti.freeColumnBasis A under it (Module.Basis.map) is the asserted basis of ker φ.
Dimension: n − rank A by finrank_ker_mulVecLin; with Mathlib LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker, rank A is the dimension of the range of φ.
acceptance: A = [[1, 2, 1], [2, 4, 0]] over ℚ: the only free column is 1, TauCeti.kernelBasis A = [(−2, 1, 0)], and A·(−2, 1, 0) = 0.
Over ZMod 2: TauCeti.kernelBasis [[1, 1], [1, 1]] = [(1, 1)] (−1 = 1).

Linear map: on the F₂-algebra F₂[X]/(X²) with basis (1, X), Frobenius x ↦ x² is F₂-linear with matrix [[1, 0], [0, 0]]; its one kernel vector (0, 1) transports to X, which spans the kernel of Frobenius, here the nilradical.
A = 0: every column is free and the β_j are the standard basis vectors; A invertible: no column is free and ker A = 0.

gaps.title: Mignotte's inequality for irreducible integer factors: source not read
gaps.detail: Mignotte, An inequality about irreducible factors of integer polynomials, J. Number Theory 30 (1988), 156–166, doi:10.1016/0022-314X(88)90014-5, Theorem 1′ and the remarks below it. Unpaywall lists a free publisher copy, but ScienceDirect answered every automated request on 2026-10-14 with a bot challenge or HTTP 403 (with a text-and-data-mining reservation), so the paper was not read. The follow-up of Glesser (Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse 11 (1990), 67–74, read on Numdam) proves a different bound (for factors of degree close to deg A) and does not contain Theorem 1′. The classical bound ‖I‖₂ ≤ C(2m, m)^{1/2}‖A‖₂ that the pinned Mahler-measure API gives is weaker by a factor exponential in m and does not suffice for Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma Lemma 3.3. Next action: read Theorem 1′ in a browser copy, record its exact hypotheses, and decompose its proof.

sourceIssues.printed: The real quadratic Pólya fields are listed as ℚ(√p) with p prime and, when the fundamental unit has norm 1, ℚ(√(pq)) with p and q prime.
sourceIssues.correction: The second family must have exactly two ramified primes: ℚ(√d) with fundamental unit of norm +1 and d = 2q (q an odd prime) or d = pq with p, q odd primes and pq ≡ 1 (mod 4). (ℚ(√p) with p ≡ 3 mod 4 already has two ramified primes and fundamental unit of norm +1.)
sourceIssues.reason: ℚ(√15) fits the printed description (15 = 3·5, fundamental unit 4 + √15 of norm 1) but is not a Pólya field: the prime 𝔭_2 above 2 (𝔭_2² = 2𝒪) is not principal, since x² − 15y² = ±2 has no solution modulo 5. Here 2, 3, 5 ramify, and Hilbert's count quoted in Leriche, Proposition 2.4, gives a Pólya group of order 2^{3−2} = 2.
